title: Comparative Field Evaluation of Active and Passive Transient‐Based Techniques for Pipeline Condition Assessment
content:
Abstract

Hydraulic transient-based techniques are increasingly applied for non-intrusive condition assessment of buried water pipelines. This study presents systematic field experiments comparing active and passive approaches within the asbestos cement water supply network at the University of Canterbury. In the active approach, controlled valve closures generated hydraulic transients analyzed via time-domain reflectometry, while the passive approach utilized cross- and auto-correlation of ambient pressure noise. Their performance was evaluated in terms of operational range, detection accuracy, and measurement duration. Results demonstrate that, for wave speed estimation, the passive approach enabled reliable time-of-flight estimation over a substantially greater sensor-to-sensor separation (projected maximum range of 980 m) than the active approach (459 m), while maintaining comparable accuracy (2%–3% error in time-of-flight). However, the active approach showed better robustness than the passive approach in identifying reflections from branches, valves, and joints, although the corresponding regression analysis showed only moderate performance. Measurement duration beyond 5 min showed only marginal benefit for passive wave speed estimation and negligible improvement for pipeline anomaly identification. Numerical simulations further clarified unexpected reflection features and provided insight into complex wave interactions. These findings highlight the complementary strengths of active and passive approaches and their potential for practical application in real-world water pipeline monitoring.
